description: O time Agreste Cósmico vai construir um app que diz ao agricultor familiar do semiárido de Pernambuco o que plantar e quando, a partir dos dados climáticos da NASA.
summary:
Orbis is a mobile-first planting advisor for family farmers in Brazil’s semi-arid Sertão. The farmer chooses a crop, a planting date and a kind of year (wetter, normal or drier) and gets a 0–100 score, the best planting window, expected rain and a plain-language verdict. Scenarios are not invented forecasts: they are averages of real years from 40 years (1985–2024) of NASA POWER data at the farmer’s location. For Serra Talhada (PE), we also compared each season’s rainfall with crop water demand (FAO-56): maize planted around Jan 21 fell short of rain in 8 of the last 10 seasons. Orbis also provides 14-day weather, alerts and an offline field logbook, in Portuguese and English.

It addresses the Field Shift challenge by turning NASA data into planting decisions on the phone farmers already have. This matters because small farmers face the greatest climate risk with the fewest tools: in Serra Talhada, average rainfall fell from 683 mm to 547 mm (1985–94 vs. 2015–24) and days at or above 35 °C rose from 118 to 145 per year.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Orbis is a pocket planting advisor for family farmers in Brazil's semi-arid Sertão. In Serra Talhada (PE), annual rainfall averages ~648 mm, but a single year can bring 218 mm or 1,299 mm, and farmers bet the whole season on the first rains. Orbis lets them test a decision before money and seed go into the ground. The farmer picks a crop (maize, beans, soybean or cassava), a planting date and a kind of year: wetter, normal or drier. The app evaluates the 12 possible planting months and returns a 0–100 score (good time, caution or high risk), the best planting window, expected rain and temperature versus the 40-year average, and practical tips. The app also has a home screen with real weather, irrigation advice and automatic alerts (heavy rain, fungal risk, wind for spraying), a 14-day weather series, a crops screen to register fields, and an offline field logbook.

HOW NASA DATA IS USED

All numbers trace to NASA POWER (Agroclimatology community): daily data for recent weather and monthly data for 1985–2024. Our scenarios are not invented forecasts: "wetter" is the average of the 10 wettest real years, "drier" the average of the 10 driest, and "normal" the average of all 40. For Serra Talhada, we also compared, season by season, the rainfall of each crop cycle with crop water demand (FAO-56: Hargreaves ETo × crop coefficient Kc) for maize, cowpea and cassava across nine planting dates. Result: rain fell short for maize in 3 of 10 seasons in 2005–2014 but 8 of 10 in 2015–2024, and maize planted around Jan 21 fell short in 8 of the last 10 seasons versus 5 for Feb 11. The app turns this into one plain sentence a farmer can read in seconds.

INTENDED IMPACT

To give the people who carry the most climate risk and have the least tooling a clear answer to "what do I plant, and on which date?", in plain language, on the phone they already own, adapting planting decisions to a shifting climate (in Serra Talhada, average rainfall fell from 683 mm to 547 mm and days at or above 35 °C rose from 118 to 145 per year between 1985–94 and 2015–24).

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

TypeScript, React Native and React 19 with Expo SDK 58 and Expo Router (one codebase for Android, iOS and web); on-device SQLite (expo-sqlite) for fields and logbook; expo-location for GPS; NASA POWER REST API (no backend, no API key); FAO-56 methodology; EAS Hosting for the live demo; bilingual PT/EN interface. AI tools (Claude) supported code, analysis and writing, and the team reviewed all decisions.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

Scenarios as years that really happened ("like the 10 driest years") instead of abstract climate models; a verdict farmers can read in one line; and a data layer that degrades honestly, falling back to saved NASA data for Serra Talhada if the network fails.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Honesty first: the NASA POWER projection API does not cover Brazil, so we removed an early heuristic that mislabeled itself as CMIP6, and when data is missing the app says so instead of guessing. We documented the limits in docs/METHODOLOGY.md: ~50 km grid data describes a region, not a field; cisterns, soil water, pests and markets are not modeled; and the method is conservative by design. Crop ranges and score thresholds are simplified reference values to be validated with Embrapa and Emater. We also designed for basic phones, offline use and plain Portuguese.

TEAM

Agreste Cósmico: Cauã Salusteano, João Manoel and Victor Leonardo
